To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
people who are interested in people are more attentive to people in the environment, whereas people who are interested more in things are more attentive to things.

people who prefer to attend to social environments (i.e., people) also have an attentional bias toward people, whereas people who prefer to focus on physical environments (i.e. things) also have an bias toward things.
people differ in the extent to which they attend to people and things, and this attentional difference relates to their interests in these categories of content.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the cognitive mechanisms that underlie individual differences in the ways people attend to and describe their environments, and how such mechanisms relate to interests and motivations.
how people attend to and represent the physical and social environments in which they live.
how attentional processes are linked to individual differences in preferences and interests.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the present study provides evidence that attentional biases toward social and physical environments are related to differential interests in people and objects.

the results of the current studies indicate that people who are more interested in people tend to attend more to social content and people who are more inclined to attend to social content tend to be more interested in people.
attentional biases toward person- and things-related content are associated with individual differences in interests in people and in things, respectively.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
individuals differ in the extent to which they attend to people or things in the environment and these individual differences are linked to their interests in the physical or social world.
people who prefer to see people tend to attend to people more, while people who prefer to attend to things tend to attend to things more.

people differ in their attention to people and things and that these differences are related to their preferences for people- and things-oriented content.
Seeing People, Seeing Things.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the way in which we attend to our environments is linked to our interests and that the way in that we describe our environments is a function of our interests.
people’s attention to people and things is not random. Instead, it is driven by individual differences in interests and motivations.
people differ in how they see their physical and social surroundings.
